summary: Expands on an experimental Encoding header field for Internet mail that supports multi-part, multi-structured messages. It replaces RFC 1154.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1505 describes an extra header for mail messages. The header lists the parts of the message body in order and names what each part contains, so a mail program can tell plain text from a compressed file or an encrypted section without guessing.

questions: encoding header field for internet mail
what is the rfc 1505 encoding header
how does the encoding header field work in email
what replaced the encoding header field
subtitle: A mail header that says what each part of a message body is made of.

tldr.problem: A mail message body could hold several kinds of content, but nothing in the message said which part was plain text and which was a compressed file or an encrypted section.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1505 adds an Encoding header field that lists the parts of the body in order, giving each one a line count and a keyword, and defines seventeen keywords covering text, files, compression, encryption and signatures.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document that obsoletes RFC 1154, and it carries an IESG note that a standards-track technology already exists in this area.

today: RFC 1505 is an Experimental document that obsoletes RFC 1154, and it has not itself been obsoleted or updated. The IESG note at the top of the memo records that a standards-track technology already exists in this area and points to RFC 1341.

sections.title: What the Encoding Header Does
sections.content:
STD 11, RFC 822, defines an electronic mail message as two parts, a message header and a message body, separated by a blank line. The Encoding header field, which this memo expands upon, permits the message body itself to be broken up further into parts, each separated from the next by a blank line. Conceptually a message then has a header part followed by one or more body parts, all separated by apparently blank lines, and each body part has an encoding type. The default, when no Encoding field is present, is a one-part message body of type Text.

The purpose of the Encoding field is to be descriptive of the content of a mail message without placing constraints on the content or requiring additional structure to appear in the body of the message that would interfere with other processing.

A similar message format is used in the network news facility, and posted articles are often transferred by gateways between news and mail. The memo argues that the Encoding field is perhaps even more useful in news, where articles are often uuencoded or shar'd and carry a number of different nested encodings of graphics images and so forth. In news the Encoding header keeps the structural information within the usually concealed article header, without affecting the visual presentation by simple news-reading software.

The memo defines an Experimental Protocol for the Internet community and requests discussion and suggestions for improvement. It replaces RFC 1154, and an IESG note at the top records that a standards-track technology already exists in this area.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail messages normally have a header and a body. This memo lets the body be split into several pieces, and adds one header line that says what each piece is. The point is to describe the content without changing the content or adding markers inside it that other software might trip over.

sections.title: The Format of the Encoding Field
sections.content:
The Encoding field consists of one or more subfields separated by commas. Each subfield corresponds to a part of the message, in the order of that part's appearance, and a subfield consists of a line count and a keyword or a series of nested keywords defining the encoding. The line count is optional in the last subfield. The formal shape of the field is [ <count> <keyword> [ <keyword> ]* , ]* [ <count> ] <keyword> [ <keyword> ]*, where a count is a decimal integer and a keyword is a single alphanumeric token starting with an alpha character.

The line count is a decimal number giving the number of text lines in the part. Parts are separated by a blank line, which is not included in the count of either the preceding or the following part, and blank lines consist only of CR/LF. The count may be zero but must be non-negative. It is always possible to tell whether a count is present, because a count always begins with a digit and a keyword always begins with a letter. The count is not required on the last or only part, so a multi-part message that consists of only one part is identical to a single-part message.

The keyword defines the encoding type. It is a common single-word name for that type and is not case-sensitive, so Encoding: 107 Text says that the next part is 107 lines of text.

Nested keywords are a series of keywords defining a multi-encoded message part. They may either be an actual series of encoding steps the encoder used to generate the part, or they may merely be used to identify the type of encoding more precisely, as in the keyword Signature. Nested keywords are parsed and generated from left to right and the order is significant: a decoding application processes the list from left to right, while an encoder generates the nested keywords in the reverse order of the actual encoding process. So a part that was tar'd, then compressed with LZW, then uuencoded is described as Encoding: 458 uuencode LZW tar (Unix binary object).

Comments enclosed in parentheses may be inserted anywhere in the field. Mail reading systems may pass the comments to their clients, but must not use them for content interpretation. Any other parameter defining the type of encoding must be contained in the body of the message or implied by a keyword in the field.
sections.plainLanguage: Each part of the body gets an entry in the header, and each entry has an optional line count and one or more keywords. The keywords are read left to right, so they read in the reverse order of the steps that produced the part.

sections.title: The Defined Encodings
sections.content:
The memo sets out principles for adding encodings. The keyword should be the most common single-word name for the encoding, including acronyms where appropriate, so that different implementors are likely to choose the same name for the same encoding; keywords should not be too general, since binary would have been a bad choice for the hex encoding. The encoding should be as free from unnecessary idiosyncrasies as possible, except where it conforms to an existing standard, and if it is a complete transformation of a source document it should use only the 7-bit ASCII printing characters, while a format that is essentially text may use the full range. Keywords beginning with X- are permanently reserved for implementation-specific use, and no standard registered encoding keyword will ever begin with X-.

The seventeen defined encodings cover plain text and everything that can be carried inside a message. Text means no particular encoded format and is presented to the user as it is; the text is ISO-10646-UTF-1, and, as specified in STD 10, RFC 821, the message is expected to consist of lines of reasonable length, at most 1000 characters, though some older implementations can use only the 7-bit subset. Text may be followed by a nested keyword, so Encoding: 496 Text, 8 Text Signature marks off a signature area that an automated file sending service can ignore.

Message means the body part is itself an Internet message, with its own header and body, and its header may be a full message header or only an Encoding field. Using it on returned mail makes a reliable automatic resending function practical, and mail transfer agents returning mail should generate an Encoding header; the message is simply appended unmodified, since MTAs are prohibited from modifying the content of messages.

Hex encodes binary data as two hexadecimal digits per byte, most significant nibble first; lines have an even number of digits, blank lines are not permitted, and the decoder must accept lines of between 2 and 1000 characters. EVFU, the electronic vertical format unit, starts each line with a one-character channel selector, originally to select a channel on a paper tape loop controlling the printer, and is sometimes called FORTRAN format. EDI-X12 and EDIFACT mark business documents formatted to those standards. FS marks a section of encoded file system objects, LZJU90 an encoded binary or text object that is both compressed and written as text, LZW the output of the Unix compress program, UUENCODE the output of the uuencode program supplied with uucp, TAR the output of the tar program supplied with Unix, and PostScript a section formatted as PostScript.

PEM and PEM-Clear mark sections encrypted with the methods of RFCs 1421 to 1424, or using the MIC-Clear encapsulation specified there; PEM does not provide detached signatures, and MIC-Clear sends integrity checks that are not encrypted, which with the right parameters can provide non-repudiation but never confidentiality. PGP marks a section encrypted with Pretty Good Privacy, or a public key block, keyring or detached signature; the keyword implies three transforms, compression, encryption and ASCII encoding, all internal to PGP. Because an eavesdropper can still see the nested type, an application worried about traffic analysis may prefer PGP Message, which conceals it. Signature marks the area of a message, usually at the end, holding the sender's name or a saying, and must always be nested and follow another keyword. URL marks zero or more references to external resources, and its specification was a work in progress in the URI working group of the IETF. SHAR marks a shell archive, whose use, although supported, is not recommended.

New keywords that are not reserved for implementation-specific use must be registered with the IANA, which acts as a central registry and may reject or modify a registration request. The request must name the keyword, give any acronyms, and include documentation that references either an external non-Internet standards document or an existing or soon-to-be RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Seventeen keywords are defined, from plain text through compressed archives to encrypted sections and detached signatures. The rules for adding more are simple: use the name people already use, keep it specific, and register it centrally.

sections.title: The File System Object Encoding
sections.content:
The FS encoding provides a standard, transportable encoding of file system objects from many different operating systems. The intent is to allow a structured set of files to be moved from one environment to another while preserving all common elements, and files can also be moved within a single environment while preserving all attributes. The representations consist of a series of nested sections, with attributes defined at the appropriate levels. Each section begins with an open bracket followed by a directive keyword and ends with a close bracket, and attributes are lines beginning with a keyword; lines that begin with a linear white space character are continuation lines.

A string-type directive or attribute may be a simple string that does not start with a quotation mark and contains no special characters or white space, in which case the string name begins at the first non-white-space character on the line following the keyword and ends at the last one. Otherwise the character string name is enclosed in quotation marks. The string itself contains characters in ISO-10646-UTF-1 but is quoted and escaped at the octet level, as elsewhere in RFC 822: octets equal to the quotation mark are escaped, as are the escape characters, and octets that are not printable are escaped with an octal representation. When an escape appears at the end of a line, the escape, the end of the line and the first character of the next line, which must be a white space character, are removed.

There are five section keywords: directory, entry, file, segment and data. The encoding may start with either a file, a directory or an entry. A directory section may contain zero or more file, entry and directory sections. A file section contains a data section or zero or more segment sections, and a segment section contains a data section or zero or more segment sections. The entry keyword represents an entry in a directory that is neither a file nor a sub-directory, such as a soft link in Unix or an access category in Primos. The segment keyword should only be used when encoding files that are actually segmented, and when encoding Macintosh files the two forks of the file are treated as segments.

The attributes defined at these levels are Display, Comment, Type, Created, Modified, Accessed, Owner, Group, ACL, Password, Block, Record and Application, and there is a date field with its own syntax and semantics. The Password attribute gives the access password for the object. Since the content of the object follows, the appearance of the password in plain text is not considered a security problem; but if the password is actually set by the decoder on a created object, the security, or the lack of it, is the responsibility of the application domain controlling the decoder, as it is for the ACL and other protections.
sections.plainLanguage: FS is a way of packing a whole directory of files into a mail message and unpacking it elsewhere with the dates, owners and permissions intact. It is written as nested blocks in square brackets, one for each directory, file and segment, with the details of each as lines underneath.

sections.title: LZJU90: A Compressed Text Encoding
sections.content:
LZJU90 is an encoding of a binary or text object that provides both compression and a representation in a text format, so that the result can travel through systems that carry only text. The compressed and encoded data is broken into lines where convenient, and lines broken every 78 characters are recommended so that they survive mailers rather than incorrectly restricting line length; the decoder must accept lines of 1 to 1000 characters each. After the data there is one final line giving the number of bytes in the original data and a CRC of the original data, which must match the byte count and CRC found during decompression. That line has the form * <count> <CRC>, where the count is a decimal number and the CRC is eight hexadecimal digits, for example * 4128076 5AC2D50E. The count used in the Encoding field in the message header is the total number of lines, including the start and end lines that begin with an asterisk.

The compression uses the Lempel-Ziv-Storer-Szymanski model of mixing pointers and literal characters. Repeat occurrences of strings of octets are replaced by pointers to the earlier occurrence. The compressed data is a mixture of unencoded literal characters and copy pointers, and there are two kinds of codeword: LITERAL, which passes the literal directly to the uncompressed output, and COPY, which goes back a given number of characters in the output and copies a given number forward to the current position. A copy length of zero indicates that the following codeword is a literal, and a copy length greater than zero indicates that it is a copy. A threshold value of 2 is subtracted from the original copy length, because the minimum copy length in this scheme is 3.

The maximum offset value is set at 32255, since larger offsets offer extremely low improvements in compression, typically less than one percent. No special encoding is done on the literal characters, but unary encoding is used for the copy length and copy offset values to improve compression, in a start-step-stop unary code where the nth codeword has n ones followed by a zero and then a field of the given size. The copy length uses a (0, 1, 7) code, leading to a maximum copy length of 256 once the threshold is included, and the copy offset uses a (9, 1, 14) code, leading to a maximum offset of 32255. Offset 0 is reserved as an end of compressed data flag.
sections.plainLanguage: LZJU90 shrinks a file and turns it into plain text at the same time, so it can be mailed. The last line carries the original size and a checksum, so the receiver can tell whether the file arrived intact.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The Security Considerations section does not set out new rules; it points at the places where they already are. The security of the content and of the receiving, decoding, system is discussed in the sections on PEM and PEM-Clear, on PGP, on SHAR and on the Password attribute, and the memo notes that the considerations mentioned there also apply to other encodings and attributes with similar functions.

Two of those are worth repeating here. The SHAR section carries a warning that, because a shell archive may contain commands the reader did not want executed, the decoder should not automatically execute decoded shell archive statements, and that the same warning applies to any future type that includes commands to be executed by the receiver. The Password attribute section explains that the appearance of a password in plain text is not considered a security problem, because the content of the object follows it, but that where the decoder actually sets a password on a created object, the security is the responsibility of the application domain controlling the decoder, as it is for access control lists and other protections.

The memo's own status is worth repeating as well. It defines an Experimental Protocol, requests discussion and suggestions for improvement, obsoletes RFC 1154, and carries the IESG note that a standards-track technology already exists in this area.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not add security rules of its own. It points to the ones that matter: do not run the commands hidden inside a shell archive, and treat the protection of a file you create yourself as the job of the program that created it.

viz.caption: THE ENCODING KEYWORDS DEFINED IN RFC 1505

items.label: Text
items.desc: No particular encoded format; presented to the user as it is. ISO-10646-UTF-1, lines of at most 1000 characters.

items.label: Message
items.desc: The body part is itself an Internet message, with its own header and body.

items.label: Hex
items.desc: Binary data as two hexadecimal digits per byte, most significant nibble first.

items.label: EVFU
items.desc: Each line begins with a one-character channel selector; sometimes called FORTRAN format.

items.label: EDI-X12
items.desc: An EDI business document formatted to the ANSI X12 standard.

items.label: EDIFACT
items.desc: An EDI business document formatted to the EDIFACT standard.

items.label: FS
items.desc: A section of encoded file system objects.

items.label: LZJU90
items.desc: An encoded binary or text object, both compressed and represented in text.

items.label: LZW
items.desc: The data produced by the Unix compress program.

items.label: UUENCODE
items.desc: The output of the uuencode program supplied as part of uucp.

items.label: PEM
items.desc: Encrypted with the methods of RFCs 1421 to 1424.

items.label: PEM-Clear
items.desc: The MIC-Clear encapsulation: integrity checks without encryption.

items.label: PGP
items.desc: Encrypted with Pretty Good Privacy, or a public key block, keyring or detached signature.

items.label: Signature
items.desc: The message signature area; must be nested and follow another keyword.

items.label: TAR
items.desc: The output of the tar program supplied as part of Unix.

items.label: PostScript
items.desc: A section formatted according to the PostScript language definition.

items.label: SHAR
items.desc: A shell archive. Supported, but not recommended.

items.label: URL
items.desc: Zero or more references to external resources.
